process: Give about five steps in order.
Name the tool or method at each step.
Finish with one real example from your work, with its result.
concept: How it works in a few steps.
When to use it and what it costs.
Where you used it, only if your profile backs it.
difference: Compare them on the same few points.
Give a one-line rule for when to use each.
Name where you used one of them.

questions.q: How do you handle messy data?
steps: Profile it first: row counts, null share per column, types, duplicates, value ranges and odd categories.
Agree what 'correct' means with whoever owns the data: which fields are required, valid ranges, the unique key.
Decide a rule per issue: drop, fix, fill or flag. Never change data silently; keep a count of what each rule touched.
Automate the rules as tests in the pipeline so the same problem is caught next time, not cleaned by hand again.
Document the decisions and monitor the counts, so a jump in bad rows raises an alert.

follow_ups.q: What if the owner does not know what is correct?
follow_ups.a: Start from how the data is used: what would break a report or a model. Propose rules, show their effect on real rows, and get a yes before applying them.

follow_ups.q: Do you ever delete bad rows?
follow_ups.a: Only with a rule everyone agreed on, and I keep them in a quarantine table with the reason, so nothing is lost and the count is visible.

questions.example_prompt: One time you found and fixed bad data, the tool you used for the checks, and the result.

questions.q: Walk me through your data preprocessing and analysis pipeline.
steps: Ingest: pull from the sources into a raw layer exactly as received, so you can always reprocess.
Validate: schema, types, nulls, duplicates and ranges, with failures counted and reported.
Clean and standardise: fix types and formats, deduplicate on the business key, handle missing values with a stated rule.
Transform: join sources, build the features or the facts and dimensions the analysis needs.
Analyse or model: explore, then answer the question or train and evaluate the model on held-out data.
Deliver and monitor: a dashboard, a table or a model, with checks that keep running after launch.

follow_ups.q: Where do most of the problems show up?
follow_ups.a: At ingestion and validation: schema changes, late files and duplicates. That is why the checks run before any transformation.

follow_ups.q: How do you make it repeatable?
follow_ups.a: Everything is code in version control, runs on a scheduler, and every load is idempotent, so a rerun gives the same result.

questions.example_prompt: Walk one of your real pipelines through these six steps, naming the tool at each step.

questions.q: How do you handle missing values?
steps: Find out why they are missing: not collected, not applicable, a join that failed, or a bug upstream.
Measure how much is missing per column and whether it is random or tied to a group.
Choose by cause: fix it upstream if it is a bug; leave it as a real 'not applicable' value; drop rows only when few and random; otherwise impute.
Impute simply first (median, most frequent, or a value per group), and add a 'was missing' flag when the missingness itself carries information.
For models, fit any imputation on training data only, to avoid leakage.

follow_ups.a: Median when the column is skewed or has outliers; mean only for roughly symmetric data.

questions.example_prompt: A column you handled and the rule you chose.

steps: Check whether each outlier is an error (a typo, a unit mix-up) or a real extreme value.
Errors: fix them at the source or remove them with a logged rule.
Real extremes: keep them, and choose methods that cope (median, robust scaling, tree models) or cap them if the analysis needs it.
Detect them with a rule that suits the data: IQR fences or z-scores for roughly normal data, domain limits otherwise.

follow_ups.a: Yes. In fraud or monitoring work the outliers are often the point.

questions.example_prompt: Where you met outliers, and whether they were errors or real.

questions.q: How do you deal with duplicate records?
steps: Define the business key that makes a record unique; exact-row duplicates are only the easy case.
Find duplicates on that key and look at how they differ (a retry, an update, two sources).
Keep one by a stated rule, usually the latest update (ROW_NUMBER over the key, ordered by updated time).
Stop them at the source: idempotent loads with MERGE or upsert on the key.

follow_ups.q: How do you find near-duplicates, like the same company spelled two ways?
follow_ups.a: Normalise first (case, punctuation, suffixes like Inc), then match on the normalised value, and review fuzzy matches before merging.

questions.q: How do you handle an imbalanced dataset?
steps: Use metrics that show the rare class: precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC, not accuracy.
Split with stratification so every set keeps the class ratio.
Try class weights first; then resampling of the training set only (undersampling, oversampling or SMOTE).
Tune the decision threshold to the business cost of a missed case versus a false alarm.

follow_ups.a: With 1% positives, predicting 'no' every time scores 99% accuracy and catches nothing.

questions.example_prompt: A rare-event problem you worked on.

questions.q: What is data leakage and how do you prevent it?
steps: Leakage is when training uses information that will not exist at prediction time, so test scores look better than reality.
Split before any fitting; fit scalers, imputers and encoders on the training data only (a pipeline object makes this automatic).
For time data, split by time, never randomly, and build features only from the past.
Be suspicious of any feature that is almost perfectly predictive, and check what it really encodes.

follow_ups.a: Predicting churn with a 'cancellation date' column: it only exists after the customer has churned.

questions.example_prompt: How you split data in one of your models.

questions.q: How do you approach exploratory data analysis?
steps: Start from the question the analysis must answer, so exploration has a direction.
Check shape, types, nulls, duplicates and ranges.
Look at each important variable alone (distributions), then in pairs (correlations, group comparisons).
Write down every surprise and check it is real, not a data error.
Summarise what you found and what it means for the next step.

follow_ups.a: Pandas for the summaries, plots for distributions, and SQL when the data stays in the warehouse.

questions.example_prompt: One finding from your own EDA that changed what you did next.

questions.q: How do you approach feature engineering?
steps: Start from what plausibly drives the outcome, with domain knowledge.
Build simple, explainable features first: ratios, counts, time since an event, rolling averages.
Encode categories suitably (one-hot for few levels, target or frequency encoding for many, fitted on training data).
Keep a feature only if it improves the validation score, and check it is available at prediction time.

follow_ups.a: Validation score with and without the feature, plus importance from the model, plus a leakage check.

questions.example_prompt: Features you built in one of your models.

questions.q: How do you validate a model before it goes to production?
steps: Hold out a test set (by time if the data is time-based) and keep it untouched until the end.
Compare against a simple baseline; a model that does not beat it is not ready.
Pick metrics that match the business cost, and look at errors by segment, not only the overall score.
Check the model on recent data and on edge cases, and confirm the features exist in production the same way.
Ship behind monitoring, with a rollback plan.

follow_ups.q: What if offline and online results disagree?
follow_ups.a: Usually a feature computed differently in production, or a shift in the data. Compare feature distributions between training and live traffic first.

questions.example_prompt: How you validated one of your models, with its numbers.

questions.q: A dashboard number is wrong. How do you debug the pipeline?
steps: Confirm the problem: what the number is, what it should be, and since when.
Walk backwards one layer at a time (dashboard, final table, staging, raw) and compare counts and sums at each.
The first layer where the numbers diverge holds the bug; look at what changed there (code, schema, a late or duplicated file).
Fix it, backfill the affected dates, and add a test that would have caught it.
Tell the people who use the number what was wrong and for which dates.

follow_ups.q: How do you avoid this next time?
follow_ups.a: Reconciliation tests between layers (row counts and key sums) and alerts when they disagree.

questions.example_prompt: A real bug you traced, how you found the root cause, and the fix.

questions.q: How do you make sure data quality stays high in a pipeline?
steps: Write the expectations down as tests: not null, unique keys, accepted values, ranges, freshness and row-count changes.
Run them on every load and stop or quarantine the load when a critical test fails.
Alert the owner with the failing test and the sample rows.
Track the pass rate over time and fix the causes upstream, not only the symptoms.

follow_ups.a: Great Expectations or dbt tests, run from the orchestrator.

questions.example_prompt: Your data quality checks and the reliability they gave.

questions.q: How do you handle late or duplicate events in streaming data?
steps: Give every event a unique id and an event time, separate from the time it arrived.
Deduplicate on the id within a time window (or with an idempotent upsert downstream).
Use event-time windows with a watermark: how long to wait for late events before closing a window.
Send events later than the watermark to a correction path, and reprocess the affected windows.

follow_ups.a: Most systems deliver at least once; making the writes idempotent gives the same end result as exactly once.

questions.example_prompt: Streaming or near-real-time work you have done.

questions.q: How would you backfill a year of data?
steps: Make the pipeline idempotent first, so rerunning a day replaces it instead of adding to it.
Run it in date partitions, oldest first, in small batches you can retry.
Limit how many run at once so the backfill does not starve normal jobs or the source system.
Check counts and totals per partition against the source as each batch finishes.

follow_ups.q: What if the logic changed during the year?
follow_ups.a: Decide with the data's users whether old days get the new logic, and record the choice.

questions.example_prompt: A backfill or reprocessing job you ran.

questions.q: The source system changed its schema. What happens to your pipeline?
steps: Detect it: schema checks on ingestion fail loudly instead of loading wrong data.
Additive changes (a new column) can usually flow through; renamed, removed or retyped columns need a code change.
Agree a data contract with the source team so changes are announced and versioned.
Keep raw data, so once the code is fixed you can reprocess.

follow_ups.a: Parquet, Avro or Delta keep the schema with the data, and table formats like Delta or Iceberg support schema evolution.

questions.example_prompt: A time a source changed under you.

questions.q: A query or Spark job is slow. How do you speed it up?
steps: Measure first: read the query plan or the Spark UI to see where the time goes.
Read less: filter early, select only needed columns, and use partition pruning.
Fix the join: index the join keys in a database, broadcast the small side in Spark, and watch for skewed keys.
Avoid repeated work: materialise expensive steps, and use incremental loads instead of full rebuilds.
Measure again to confirm the gain.

follow_ups.a: A few keys hold most of the rows, so one task does most of the work. Fixes: salting the key, or handling the hot keys separately.

questions.example_prompt: A performance improvement you made, with the before and after.

questions.q: How do you monitor a model in production?
steps: Watch the inputs: feature distributions against training (PSI or a KS test) to catch drift.
Watch the outputs: prediction distribution and confidence.
Watch the outcome when labels arrive: accuracy or error over time, and by segment.
Alert on thresholds, and have a retraining and rollback plan.

follow_ups.q: What is data drift versus concept drift?
follow_ups.a: Data drift: the inputs change. Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and the outcome changes, so the same inputs now mean something else.

questions.example_prompt: Drift detection or monitoring you built.

questions.definition: A model that predicts a number as a weighted sum of the inputs plus a constant.
questions.picture: Drawing the straight line that sits closest to a cloud of points.
how: Choose the weights that make the squared errors between predictions and real values as small as possible.
Each weight says how much the prediction moves when that input goes up by one, holding the others fixed.
questions.use_when: A first model for a numeric target, and whenever you need to explain the effect of each input.
questions.trade_offs: Simple, fast and explainable, but it assumes a straight-line relationship and is hurt by outliers and strongly correlated inputs.

follow_ups.a: The share of the target's variance the model explains; it never goes down when you add features, so use adjusted R-squared or a validation score.

questions.definition: A classification model that predicts the probability of a yes/no outcome.
questions.picture: Linear regression whose output is squeezed between 0 and 1 by an S-shaped curve.
how: Compute a weighted sum of the inputs.
Pass it through the sigmoid to get a probability.
Train by maximising the likelihood of the real labels (log loss).
Pick a threshold to turn probabilities into decisions.
questions.use_when: A strong, explainable baseline for classification.
questions.trade_offs: Fast and explainable, but it draws a straight boundary unless you add interaction or transformed features.

follow_ups.q: Why is it called regression if it classifies?
follow_ups.a: It regresses the log-odds of the outcome on the inputs; the classification comes from the threshold.

questions.definition: A model that makes a prediction through a sequence of yes/no questions about the inputs.
questions.picture: A game of twenty questions that ends in an answer.
how: At each step, pick the split that best separates the target (Gini or entropy for classes, squared error for numbers).
Repeat on each branch until a stopping rule (depth, minimum rows).
A leaf predicts the majority class or the average value.
questions.use_when: When you need rules people can read, or as the building block of forests and boosting.
questions.trade_offs: Easy to read and needs no scaling, but a single deep tree overfits and changes a lot with small data changes.

follow_ups.q: How do you stop it overfitting?
follow_ups.a: Limit depth, require a minimum number of rows per leaf, or prune.

questions.definition: An ensemble of many decision trees, each trained on a random sample of the rows and a random subset of the features, that vote or average.
questions.picture: Asking a hundred people who each saw part of the data, then taking the majority: individual mistakes cancel out.
how: Draw a bootstrap sample of the rows for each tree.
At each split, consider only a random subset of the features.
Grow many deep trees.
Average their predictions, or take the majority vote.
questions.use_when: A strong default for tabular data with little tuning.
questions.trade_offs: Robust and hard to overfit, but bigger, slower and harder to explain than one tree, and it cannot predict beyond the range of the training targets.

follow_ups.a: Many small rule-based voters, each trained on a different random slice of the data, and the final answer is their vote.
Each tree skips about a third of the rows; scoring each row with the trees that did not see it gives a free validation estimate.

questions.definition: An ensemble that builds small trees one after another, each one correcting the errors of the ones before it.
questions.picture: A team where each new member studies only the mistakes the team still makes.
how: Start with a simple prediction.
Fit a small tree to the current errors (the gradient of the loss).
Add it with a small learning rate.
Repeat for many rounds, stopping when the validation score stops improving.
questions.use_when: When you need the best accuracy on tabular data and can spend time tuning.
questions.trade_offs: Often the most accurate on tabular data, but more sensitive to its settings and easier to overfit than a random forest.

follow_ups.a: Learning rate, number of trees (with early stopping), tree depth, and row and column sampling.

questions.definition: An unsupervised method that splits data into k groups so that points are close to their group's centre.
questions.picture: Placing k flags in a field so everyone walks to the nearest flag, then moving each flag to the middle of its crowd.
how: Pick k starting centres.
Assign each point to its nearest centre.
Move each centre to the mean of its points.
Repeat until assignments stop changing.
questions.use_when: Segmentation (customers, products) when groups are roughly round and similar in size.
questions.trade_offs: Simple and fast, but you must choose k, it needs scaled features, and it struggles with odd-shaped or very unequal clusters.

follow_ups.a: The elbow of the within-cluster error curve, silhouette scores, and whether the groups make sense to the business.

questions.definition: A model's error comes from being too simple (bias) or too sensitive to the training data (variance); reducing one tends to raise the other.
questions.picture: Bias is always missing the target in the same direction; variance is hitting all over the place.
how: Simple models: high bias, low variance (underfit).
Complex models: low bias, high variance (overfit).
Aim for the complexity where validation error is lowest.
questions.use_when: To explain why a model underfits or overfits and what to change.
questions.trade_offs: More data mainly reduces variance; more features or a more flexible model mainly reduce bias.

follow_ups.q: How do you tell which one you have?
follow_ups.a: Both training and validation error high: bias. Training error low and validation error much higher: variance.

questions.q: What is overfitting and how do you prevent it?
questions.definition: When a model learns noise in the training data, so it scores well there and badly on new data.
questions.picture: Memorising last year's exam answers instead of learning the subject.
how: Detect it with a gap between training and validation scores.
Prevent it with more data, simpler models, regularisation (L1/L2, dropout), early stopping, and cross-validation.
questions.use_when: Always: every model is checked on data it did not train on.
questions.trade_offs: Too much regularisation causes underfitting instead, so tune it on validation data.

follow_ups.a: Adds a penalty for large weights, which pushes the model towards simpler explanations.

questions.definition: Estimating how a model will do on new data by training and testing it several times on different splits.
questions.picture: Taking several practice exams on different topics instead of trusting one.
how: Split the data into k folds.
Train on k-1 folds and test on the remaining one.
Repeat so each fold is the test once, and average the scores.
questions.use_when: Model selection and tuning when data is limited.
questions.trade_offs: More reliable than one split but k times the training cost; for time data use time-based splits, not random folds.

follow_ups.q: Is a test set still needed?
follow_ups.a: Yes. Cross-validation guides choices; a final untouched test set gives the honest score.

questions.definition: Precision: of the cases flagged positive, how many really were. Recall: of the real positives, how many were caught. F1: the harmonic mean of the two.
questions.picture: A fishing net: precision is how much of the catch is the fish you wanted; recall is how much of that fish you caught.
how: Precision = TP / (TP + FP).
Recall = TP / (TP + FN).
F1 = 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall).
questions.use_when: Classification with an imbalanced or costly-error problem.
questions.trade_offs: Raising the threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall; the business cost decides where to sit.

follow_ups.a: When missing a case is expensive: fraud, disease screening, safety.

questions.definition: The area under the curve of true positive rate against false positive rate across all thresholds: the chance the model ranks a random positive above a random negative.
questions.picture: How well the model sorts the cases, before you choose where to draw the line.
how: Score every case.
For every threshold, compute the true and false positive rates.
Plot them and measure the area: 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect.
questions.use_when: Comparing models independent of the threshold.
questions.trade_offs: It can look good on heavily imbalanced data while precision is poor; use PR-AUC there.

follow_ups.a: PR-AUC, because positives are rare and precision matters.

questions.definition: A table of a classifier's predictions against the real labels: true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives.
questions.picture: A scorecard that shows not just how often the model is wrong, but how.
how: Rows are the real classes, columns the predicted ones (or the reverse).
Every metric (accuracy, precision, recall) is computed from its cells.
questions.use_when: Any time you report a classifier, to show which mistakes it makes.
questions.trade_offs: It depends on the threshold chosen.

follow_ups.q: Which cell is a false negative?
follow_ups.a: A real positive the model predicted as negative: a missed case.

questions.definition: The probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if there were really no effect (the null hypothesis).
questions.picture: How surprising your data would be in a world where nothing changed.
how: State the null hypothesis.
Compute the test statistic from the data.
The p-value is the share of results at least this extreme under the null.
Below a threshold set in advance (often 0.05), reject the null.
questions.use_when: Hypothesis tests and A/B tests.
questions.trade_offs: It is not the probability that the null is true, and it says nothing about how big or important the effect is.

follow_ups.q: What is a type I error?
follow_ups.a: Rejecting a true null: a false alarm. Type II is missing a real effect.

questions.definition: A range built so that, if you repeated the study many times, 95% (for a 95% interval) of the ranges would contain the true value.
questions.picture: A margin of error around an estimate.
how: Estimate the value.
Estimate its standard error.
Take the estimate plus and minus about 1.96 standard errors for 95%.
questions.use_when: Reporting any estimate, so people see its uncertainty.
questions.trade_offs: Wider with less data or more noise; more data narrows it.

follow_ups.q: Can you say there is a 95% chance the true value is inside?
follow_ups.a: Strictly, no: the method captures it 95% of the time. In practice people say it that way.

questions.q: How do you run an A/B test?
questions.definition: A controlled experiment that randomly splits users between the current version and a change to measure the change's effect.
questions.picture: A fair coin decides who gets the new version, so the only difference between the groups is the change.
how: Pick one primary metric and the smallest effect worth detecting.
Compute the sample size (power analysis) before starting.
Randomise users, run for the planned time, and do not stop early when it looks good.
Test the difference, check guardrail metrics, and decide.
questions.use_when: Any product or model change where you can split traffic.
questions.trade_offs: Needs enough traffic and time; peeking early and testing many metrics both inflate false positives.

follow_ups.q: What is a sample ratio mismatch?
follow_ups.a: The groups are not the planned sizes, which signals a bug in assignment; the result cannot be trusted until it is fixed.

questions.definition: The average of many independent samples is approximately normally distributed, whatever the shape of the original data.
questions.picture: Single dice rolls are flat, but averages of many rolls pile up in a bell around 3.5.
how: Take repeated samples of size n.
Compute each sample's mean.
Those means form a bell curve that narrows as n grows.
questions.use_when: It is why confidence intervals and many tests work on non-normal data.
questions.trade_offs: Needs reasonably large samples and independent observations; very heavy tails need more data.

questions.definition: A warehouse design with one fact table of measurable events in the middle, joined to dimension tables that describe them.
questions.picture: A receipt (the fact) linked to the customer, the product, the store and the date (the dimensions).
how: Choose the grain: what one row in the fact table means.
Put the measures (amounts, counts) in the fact table with keys to each dimension.
Put the descriptive attributes in the dimension tables.
questions.use_when: Analytics and BI, where queries filter and group by descriptive attributes.
questions.trade_offs: Simple, fast queries, at the cost of some duplicated data in the dimensions.

follow_ups.a: What one fact row represents, such as one order line per day. Choosing it first stops double counting.

questions.definition: Ways of handling dimension attributes that change over time, such as a customer moving city.
questions.picture: Deciding whether history is overwritten or kept.
how: Type 1: overwrite; no history.
Type 2: add a new row with valid-from and valid-to dates and a current flag; full history.
Type 3: keep the previous value in an extra column; limited history.
questions.use_when: Type 2 whenever reports must show what was true at the time.
questions.trade_offs: Type 2 keeps history but grows the table and needs date-aware joins.

follow_ups.q: How do you join a fact to a type 2 dimension?
follow_ups.a: On the business key where the fact's date falls between valid-from and valid-to.

questions.definition: One that gives the same result whether it runs once or many times for the same input.
questions.picture: Pressing a lift button twice still calls one lift.
how: Write with MERGE or upsert on a key, or overwrite a whole partition, instead of appending.
Make each run depend only on its inputs and its date, not on what ran before.
questions.use_when: Every production pipeline: retries and backfills then become safe.
questions.trade_offs: Upserts cost more than appends, but avoid duplicates and manual clean-up.

follow_ups.q: How does it help a backfill?
follow_ups.a: You can rerun any date range and it replaces those days instead of doubling them.

questions.q: What is partitioning, and why does it matter?
questions.definition: Splitting a table's data into parts by a column (often date), so queries read only the parts they need.
questions.picture: Filing papers into folders by month so you open one folder instead of the whole cabinet.
how: Choose a column queries filter on, usually a date.
Store each value's rows separately.
Queries that filter on it skip the other partitions (pruning).
questions.use_when: Large tables with a common filter.
questions.trade_offs: Too many tiny partitions slow things down; choose a column with moderate cardinality.

follow_ups.a: Partitioning splits the data into separate parts; clustering or sort keys order the data inside them. They are often used together.

questions.q: Why is Parquet used so much?
questions.definition: A columnar file format: data is stored column by column, compressed, with the schema and statistics in the file.
questions.picture: Reading one column of a spreadsheet without opening the other columns.
how: Values of one column are stored together, so they compress well.
Queries read only the columns they need.
Per-chunk min/max statistics let readers skip data that cannot match.
questions.use_when: Analytics storage in data lakes and lakehouses.
questions.trade_offs: Fast to read and small, but not suited to frequent single-row updates; table formats such as Delta or Iceberg add that on top.

follow_ups.a: Parquet for analytics: typed, compressed, columnar. CSV only for simple exchange.

questions.definition: Capturing the inserts, updates and deletes from a source database as a stream of changes, usually from its transaction log.
questions.picture: Reading the database's own diary instead of photographing the whole database every night.
how: A connector (such as Debezium) reads the log.
Each change becomes an event with the before and after values.
Downstream, the changes are merged into the target table.
questions.use_when: Keeping a warehouse in near real time with a busy source, without heavy full extracts.
questions.trade_offs: Low load on the source and fresh data, but more moving parts; deletes and schema changes need care.

questions.q: What does an orchestrator like Airflow do?
questions.definition: It schedules and runs pipeline tasks in dependency order, retries failures and shows what ran.
questions.picture: A conductor who starts each section when the one before it has finished.
how: Define tasks and their dependencies as a DAG (directed acyclic graph).
The scheduler runs each task when its upstream tasks succeed.
Failures retry, alert, and can be rerun for a given date.
questions.use_when: Any pipeline with several dependent steps on a schedule.
questions.trade_offs: It orchestrates work; heavy processing should run in the warehouse or Spark, not inside the orchestrator.

follow_ups.a: A set of tasks with one-way dependencies and no loops, so there is always a valid order to run them.

questions.definition: Giving a language model relevant documents retrieved at question time, so it answers from them instead of from memory alone.
questions.picture: An open-book exam: the model looks up the right pages before answering.
how: Split the documents into chunks and embed them.
Embed the question and retrieve the most similar chunks (often with reranking).
Put them in the prompt and ask the model to answer only from them, citing them.
questions.use_when: Answers grounded in private or frequently changing data.
questions.trade_offs: Cheaper to update than fine-tuning and can cite sources, but answers are only as good as the retrieval.

follow_ups.q: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
follow_ups.a: Separately: retrieval (did the right chunks come back) and the answer (is it correct and supported by those chunks).

follow_ups.q: What if retrieval returns nothing useful?
follow_ups.a: Have the model say it does not know instead of guessing.

questions.definition: Lists of numbers that represent text (or images) so that similar meanings end up close together.
questions.picture: Coordinates on a map of meaning.
how: A model turns each text into a fixed-length vector.
Similarity is measured with cosine similarity or dot product.
questions.use_when: Semantic search, RAG retrieval, clustering, recommendations and deduplication.
questions.trade_offs: They capture meaning well, but exact terms and IDs are better matched with keyword search; hybrid search combines both.

questions.definition: A store that indexes embeddings so you can quickly find the nearest ones to a query vector.
questions.picture: A library catalogue sorted by meaning instead of by title.
how: Store each vector with its text and metadata.
Build an approximate nearest-neighbour index (such as HNSW).
Query with a vector, filter by metadata, and return the top matches.
questions.use_when: RAG and semantic search over many documents.
questions.trade_offs: Approximate search trades a little accuracy for big speed; for small data a plain array or pgvector in Postgres is enough.

questions.q: What is hallucination, and how do you reduce it?
questions.definition: When a model states something fluent and confident that is not true or not supported by its sources.
questions.picture: A confident guess presented as a fact.
how: Ground answers in retrieved sources and ask for citations.
Allow 'I don't know'.
Check outputs mechanically where possible (numbers, names, tool results) instead of trusting the model.
Measure the hallucination rate on a test set.
questions.use_when: Any production use where wrong answers cost something.
questions.trade_offs: Grounding and checks reduce it but never remove it, so the checks matter more than the prompt.

questions.definition: A model that works in a loop: it decides on an action, calls a tool (search, code, an API), reads the result, and continues until the task is done.
questions.picture: An assistant that can look things up and use software, not just talk.
how: Give the model tools with clear descriptions.
It plans a step and calls a tool.
The real tool result goes back into the context.
It repeats until it has an answer or hits a limit.
questions.use_when: Tasks that need live data or several steps.
questions.trade_offs: Flexible, but slower, costlier and harder to test; needs step limits, cost limits and checks on every tool result.

follow_ups.a: A pattern where the model alternates reasoning and acting: a thought, a tool call, the observation, and so on.

questions.q: What are tokens and the context window?
questions.definition: Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads (roughly three quarters of an English word); the context window is the most tokens it can take in at once, prompt and answer together.
questions.picture: The model's working memory for one conversation.
how: Everything (instructions, documents, history, answer) must fit in the window.
Cost and speed scale with the tokens used.
questions.use_when: Planning prompts, RAG chunk sizes and costs.
questions.trade_offs: Long contexts are convenient but cost more and models can miss details in the middle, so retrieve only what is needed.

questions.definition: Further training a pre-trained model on your own examples so it learns a style, a format or a narrow task.
questions.picture: Sending a skilled employee on a course for your company's way of working.
how: Collect high-quality input and output examples.
Train (often a light method such as LoRA) on them.
Evaluate against the base model on held-out examples.
questions.use_when: A consistent format or behaviour that prompting cannot reliably get, or a smaller, cheaper model for one task.
questions.trade_offs: Costs data and training time and must be redone for new facts; it teaches behaviour better than knowledge.

questions.definition: Measuring performance against a fixed, shared standard so results can be compared. For models: a standard test set and metric. For systems: a repeatable load test of speed or cost.
questions.picture: A standard exam everyone takes, so scores are comparable.
how: Fix the test set or workload and the metric.
Run every candidate the same way.
Compare the scores, and repeat runs for systems to see the spread.
questions.use_when: Choosing between models, tools or designs.
questions.trade_offs: Public benchmarks may not match your task and can leak into training data, so evaluate on your own data as well.

follow_ups.q: How did you benchmark something yourself?
follow_ups.a: Say what you held fixed, what you measured, and the result.

questions.definition: Reusing the processed form of a long, unchanged prompt prefix across calls, so repeated calls cost less and start faster.
questions.picture: Not re-reading the whole manual every time you ask a question about it.
how: Put the stable part (instructions, documents) first and the changing part last.
Mark the stable prefix as cacheable.
Later calls with the same prefix read it from the cache at a lower price.
questions.use_when: Many calls that share the same long context.
questions.trade_offs: Only exact prefixes are reused, and caches expire after a short time.

rows: Many models trained in parallel on random samples
Models trained in sequence, each fixing the last one's errors
questions.rule: Bagging for a robust default; boosting for the last bit of accuracy.
Random forest when you want good results fast; boosting when accuracy is worth the tuning time.

rows: Pushes some weights to exactly zero
questions.rule: L1 to drop features, L2 to keep them all but smaller; elastic net mixes both.

rows: Of what I flagged, how much was right?
Of what was there, how much did I catch?
questions.rule: Choose by which mistake costs more, then move the threshold.
Labels available: supervised. No labels: unsupervised, often to explore or create features.
Decide by the type of the answer you need.

rows: The information given at question time
Facts that change or are private
A consistent style or narrow task
questions.rule: Start with prompting, add RAG for knowledge, fine-tune only for behaviour prompting cannot get.

rows: A fixed, shared test set or workload
Your own task's data and criteria
Compare against others on a standard
Decide whether it works for your use
May not match your task; can leak into training
Needs effort to build a good test set
questions.rule: Benchmarks to shortlist, your own evaluation to decide.

rows: Load raw, transform inside the warehouse
The warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery) with SQL, often dbt
questions.rule: ELT is the default with a cloud warehouse; ETL when data must be cleaned or masked before it lands.
Use streaming only when the business needs fresher data than a schedule gives.

questions.q: Data lake versus warehouse versus lakehouse?
rows: Open files with table features on top
One copy for both BI and ML
questions.rule: A lakehouse aims to give warehouse reliability on lake storage.
Run the business on OLTP; analyse it on OLAP.
Star schema is the usual default for analytics; snowflake when dimensions are huge or shared.
